newsitem.title: USA: Clinton, Dole camps wrangle over debates.
newsitem.headline: Clinton, Dole camps wrangle over debates.

text.p: Campaign aides for President Bill Clinton and Republican challenger Bob Dole on Wednesday squabbled over arrangements for the presidential debates, with Clinton's spokesman saying the Dole team was putting the encounters in jeopardy.
However, Clinton himself took a positive view. "There will be debates, I'm sure of it," he said when reporters asked him about the controversy.

Clinton campaign spokesman Joe Lockhart said the Dole team wanted to stage the second presidential debate scheduled for Oct. 16 in San Diego two hours earlier than agreed in order to avoid clashing with a baseball playoff game.

The Dole camp also wanted the candidates to stand on a podium behind lecterns instead of on the same level as the audience, Lockhart said. The San Diego debate was initially planned as a "town hall meeting" where the candidates answer questions from undecided voters.

"What they're trying to do is renegotiate several points. Our view is we have signed the agreement and we will not reopen it," said Lockhart, who was accompanying Clinton on a campaign trip to Pennsylvania.
"They have had the agreement for 48 hours. They haven't signed it. They are now putting the debates in jeopardy," he added.
Dole campaign spokesman Nelson Warfield said the Dole team was asking for the lecterns because Dole's Second World War wounds made it hard for him to take notes.
"Given his war wounds, Sen. Dole has specific concerns about how he would take notes," he said. "I can't imagine President Clinton would want to take advantage of his war wounds."
Lockhart later retorted that the lectern issue was a "red herring."

He said the opposing camps had agreed to a "three-sided structure" at the San Diego debate that the candidates could use to take notes or lean against. "In the contract there is a provision that says the structure will be designed by the (presidential debate) commission and approved by both campaigns," he said.
In the 1992 town hall meeting between Clinton, President George Bush and independent Ross Perot, the three candidates sat on bar stools and took no notes.
As for changing the time of the debate, Dole officials said that was in everyone's best interests to ensure as large a television audience as possible.

But Lockart said the Dole campaign wanted to change an arrangement it demanded in the first place. "It was the Dole campaign that pushed for the debate on the 16th. Our preference was for the 13th," he said.
Warfield said Dole campaign officials were still reviewing the draft agreement before signing it because it contained new elements not agreed to in the negotiations.

The two sides agreed on Saturday to hold two presidential and one vice presidential debate. The first presidential encounter is scheduled for Oct. 6 in Hartford, Connecticut, the second for Oct. 16 in San Diego. The vice presidential debate is supposed to take place Oct. 9 in St. Petersburg, Florida.
The sides also agreed to exclude Perot, now the Reform Party's presidential candidate, and all other candidates from the debates, each of which will be 90 minutes long.
